_comment: Mutations for the readiness probes and the two health endpoints, scored against BOTH harnesses. http_run.sh has the endpoints and covers the wiring — the cache, the status code, the rollup. health_run.sh has the probes with every input supplied, and covers everything the HTTP one structurally cannot reach: the mutator restarts the tier before each run, so the process is always inside its startup grace, and the harness environment has email on, a valid licence and a healthy disk. Seventeen of these survived an HTTP-only run for that reason. Several are about the vocabulary rather than the logic — `disabled` versus `unconfigured`, `warn` versus `critical` — because those distinctions are the whole product of a health endpoint and the easiest thing to flatten by accident.

mutations.name: warn flips readiness to 503
mutations._why: Only critical pages. A disk at 85% is yellow on a dashboard; answering 503 for it would have every uptime monitor paging on a volume that needs resizing next month.
mutations.old: let ready = !probes.iter().any(|(_, p)| p.is_critical());

mutations.name: nothing flips readiness
mutations._why: The other direction: an endpoint that always answers 200 tells an uptime monitor nothing at all.
mutations.old: let ready = !probes.iter().any(|(_, p)| p.is_critical());

mutations.name: the licence probe can page
mutations._why: Never critical, by design: an unlicensed AI feature is not a Command Center outage and must not flip readiness. It is surfaced on `detailed` for an operator to notice, and nowhere else.
mutations.old: let status = if licensed && reachable == "true" { "ok" } else { "warn" };
mutations.new: let status = if licensed && reachable == "true" { "ok" } else { "critical" };

mutations.name: a coasting licence reports healthy
mutations._why: Reachability is not validity. A revoked licence behind a perfectly reachable service, and a valid one coasting on grace while the service is down, both have to stop short of ok.
mutations.old: let status = if licensed && reachable == "true" { "ok" } else { "warn" };

mutations.name: the disk thresholds are swapped
mutations._why: 95 pages, 80 warns. Inverted, a nearly full volume is yellow and a half-full one is red.

mutations.name: free bytes are read as available-to-root
mutations._why: `shutil.disk_usage` reports `f_bavail` — what an unprivileged process can actually have — not `f_bfree`, which includes the reserved blocks. On a filesystem with a 5% reserve the two differ by gigabytes.
mutations.old: let free = stat.f_bavail as u64 * frsize;
mutations.new: let free = stat.f_bfree as u64 * frsize;

mutations.name: used bytes are total minus available
mutations._why: Used is total minus FREE, not total minus available: the reserved blocks are not in use, they are merely unavailable, and counting them as used inflates the percentage that decides whether someone is paged.
mutations.old: let used = (stat.f_blocks as u64 - stat.f_bfree as u64) * frsize;
mutations.new: let used = (stat.f_blocks as u64 - stat.f_bavail as u64) * frsize;

mutations.name: the disk percentage is not rounded to one place
mutations._why: `round(pct, 1)`. An unrounded float is a different JSON number, and this one is rendered on a status page.
mutations.old: crate::pyrepr::round_to((used as f64 / total as f64) * 100.0, 1)

mutations.name: a self-hosted install reports Clerk unconfigured
mutations._why: `disabled` and `unconfigured` are different answers to an operator: one is a deliberate choice, the other is a setup step they forgot.

mutations.name: a self-hosted install calls Clerk anyway
mutations._why: There is no Clerk account in local mode, so the call cannot succeed — it would report critical on every poll of a perfectly healthy install.

mutations.name: an empty licence timestamp reports as empty rather than null
mutations._why: `x or None` — a falsy string becomes null in the JSON, and a status page rendering "" for "never" is a different answer.

mutations.name: the probe payload nests instead of flattening
mutations._why: `{"status": …, **data}` — the payload sits BESIDE the status, not under a key. Every consumer of this endpoint reads it flat.

mutations.name: readiness answers 200 when a probe is critical
mutations._why: The whole point of this endpoint over `detailed`: uptime monitors read HTTP status, not JSON.

mutations.name: the readiness cache is never used
mutations._why: Thirty seconds of cache is what keeps a swarm of pollers — two uptime monitors, a status page and the admin panel — from hammering Clerk on every request.

mutations.name: nocache is ignored
mutations._why: The diagnostic escape hatch. Ignoring it hands an on-call engineer a cached answer from before the incident.
mutations.old: let nocache = q.bool("nocache", false);

mutations.name: the cache never expires
mutations._why: A TTL that never elapses freezes the first answer the process ever gave, which is the worst possible thing for a health endpoint to do.

mutations.name: an unreadable nocache is a silent false
mutations._why: FastAPI answers 422 for a bool it cannot coerce. Silently defaulting hands back a cached answer while the caller believes they bypassed the cache.
mutations.old: q.finish()?;

mutations.name: detailed rolls warn up as unhealthy
mutations._why: Warn-tier signals colour the dashboard; critical-tier ones page. Collapsing them means a disk at 85% reads the same as a dead database.

mutations.name: resend being off degrades the rollup
mutations._why: An install running without email is a configuration choice, not a failure mode. Letting it degrade the rollup paints every self-hosted install yellow forever — which is why resend is not an input to `rollup` at all.

mutations.name: a failed queue count reports zero
mutations._why: -1 says "we do not know". Zero says "the queue is empty", which is a claim, and the wrong one.
mutations.old: pub const UNKNOWN_QUEUE_DEPTH: i64 = -1;

mutations._why: A backlog past a hundred thousand pending writes means the flush loop is failing quietly, which is the only symptom it has.
